item.title: If you are building AI for finance, get out while you can
item.description:
LLMs are good with probabilistic logic (words), but not as good with deterministic logic (numbers).

As oppose to what everybody thought 3 years ago, LLMs are not very good with finance. Makes sense when you think about it as AI in 2025 still rely heavily on language transformers, and transformers are more or less probability calculators.

Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. 1 wrong word in the bylaws can break your entire company. Accounting is more precise, it tolerates less mistakes, and the rules that govern it are much less option to intrepretation.

In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future.

In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate.

It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. A football player such as Arbeloa, who ranks in the 80th percentile, is not remotely comparable to someone in the 90th percentile. Now imagine a player who is better than 99% of all football players who ever lived; that superstar is on an entirely different level, and Arbeloa would lose 0–10 to him every single time.

All of which without mentioning the 99.99th percentile, where the gap becomes unimaginable to human minds. Accounting follows the same power law; 99% accuracy rate might sound close to perfect, but across 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, but how can we know which ones are going to be bad. Its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal. Also, all the major labs are going after accounting after they finish with coding, so margins are going down fast.

Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Its not even the hullication part that scares them, but the part where the Ai missed something. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story. Its about accountibility more than anything else.

Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller. Courts won't allow an Ai attorney to present a case no matter how good it was at the job.

item.title: Show HN: Instant – Local AI search with a 95% hit rate (uses Perplexity models)
item.description:
Hi HN!

Instant Search is the first accurate local AI file search that uses the latest embedding models from Perplexity to find the exact file (and page) with the content you’re looking for with a 95% hit rate.

Search never worked properly, especially with local files. Now, you can find the right image, document, or Obsidian file in seconds. Looking for your driver’s license? Just type “driver’s license”. Looking for a particular note? Just explain the context.

Why not Finder/Spotlight?

Spotlight is just a keyword search. It doesn’t understand file content. Instant finds the exact file you’re describing in under a second.

Why not RAG?

Traditional RAG models give you a single embedding vector per entire body of text. That means either you have a vector that’s not detailed enough to give you an accurate semantic representation, or it’s too precise and doesn’t contain enough surrounding context. Instant circumvents these problems by relying on a bidirectional late-interaction embedding model that works flawlessly.

How much space does indexing need? An average library of content needs less than 1GB of disk space.

Check it out, share with friends, and let me know your feedback! It's free.
